## Overview

This short demo shows the kind of lightweight analysis that works well in a Quarto case
study: create a small data set, calculate a few marketing metrics, and turn the result
into a chart that can be discussed with a non-technical audience.

## Campaign performance

```{python}
#| label: tbl-campaign-performance
#| tbl-cap: "Illustrative campaign performance by channel"

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

campaigns = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "channel": ["Search", "Social", "Email", "Display", "Affiliate"],
        "spend": [18000, 14000, 3500, 9000, 7000],
        "conversions": [720, 420, 210, 180, 260],
        "revenue": [64800, 33600, 18900, 13500, 23400],
    }
)

campaigns["cost_per_conversion"] = campaigns["spend"] / campaigns["conversions"]
campaigns["roas"] = campaigns["revenue"] / campaigns["spend"]
campaigns.sort_values("roas", ascending=False)
```

The table gives a quick performance readout. Email has a small spend base but strong
efficiency, while Search carries more volume.

## Return on ad spend

```{python}
#| label: fig-campaign-roas
#| fig-cap: "Return on ad spend by channel"
#| fig-alt: "ROAS: Email, Affiliate, Search, Social, Display, in descending order."

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ordered = campaigns.sort_values("roas")

ax.barh(ordered["channel"], ordered["roas"], color="#0e4e68")
ax.axvline(1, color="#666666", linewidth=1)
ax.set_title("Return on ad spend by channel")
ax.set_xlabel("Revenue / spend")
ax.set_ylabel("")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

plt.show()
```

## Interpretation

For a real readout, this would be followed by caveats: attribution window,
incrementality, audience overlap, campaign objective, and whether the next decision is
about scaling spend or improving creative.
